activity.title: I'm happy to share that my team won 1st place at Hack the Town hackathon sponsored by Google Play , presented by Hack the Hood ! We won $1800 :) and what's more exciting is to see my first app published on the Google Play Store! This was a 2-day event and my first hackathon experience. We built TrashGO, a community-driven platform designed to make neighborhood cleanups more accessible, engaging, and rewarding. Our goal with TrashGO was to create a platform where anyone can report local trash, discover cleanup events, and organize meetups to work together to clean up their communities. A big inspiration behind TrashGO was Pokémon GO. We wanted to take this idea of people meeting together and catching Pokemon and apply it to cleaning up neighborhoods. We plan to build upon this with gamified points and a rewards system that encourages users to participate, stay active, and be engaged. We also want to collaborate with local restaurants and businesses to offer benefits for members. In just two days, we built the full user experience, including authentication, an interactive map, event pages, progress tracking, event creation, scheduling, location finder, personal activity tracking, and an impact dashboard! Since this was my first hackathon, I learned so much about building under a tight deadline, turning an idea into a working product, designing around user needs, and collaborating with an amazing team. The most important lesson I learnt is building a good product isn't just about writing code or coming up with a solution, rather finding a real problem that solves a need while contributing to a meaningful cause and it's broader impact. A huge thank you to our awesome coach, Zain Shafique , for guiding us throughout the hackathon, helping us work through the idea, and pushing us to build TrashGO. I'm happy to share that Neev Tamboli , Shivansh Bansal , and I won 1st place in 2 different tracks at the Daytona Hack Sprint! (1st overall and Best Use of Fireworks). We built a continuation of SubStrata, a satellite land-cover classification agent that gets more accurate over time. Aayush Gandhi , Neev Tamboli and I had built this project earlier, but we decided to build on it at this hackathon! Space agencies and research teams often rely on general-purpose land cover models that plateau in accuracy, and improving them typically requires either expensive proprietary retraining or slow, manual review by researchers. Substrata is a space agency oriented land cover classification tool that uses a recursive self-improvement loop between two AI models to push satellite imagery classification accuracy from 42% to 91%. Gemini 3.5 Flash classifies and segments Sentinel-2 and Dynamic World satellite imagery pulled through Google Earth Engine, while a second model audits its output against ground-truth labels, flags discrepancies, and pushes corrections into a persistent memory layer that Gemini references on every subsequent image. At this hackathon, we implemented Fireworks AI to host the vision classifier that scores every satellite patch, alongside using it to power LLM tool calls throughout the pipeline. We rebuilt our scoring system on Braintrust instead of relying on our own math, and the results spoke for themselves: our graph memory approach hit 89% accuracy versus 64% for raw retrieval. We also rebuilt our heuristic panel using CopilotKit, so you can watch the model write out its reasoning live and see the accuracy graph climb in real time as it learns. To make the whole system more resilient, we moved each batch into its own Daytona sandbox, so one bad batch can no longer take the entire pipeline down. Before submitting, we ran everything through CodeRabbit for a final review pass on the code we shipped. Special thanks to Sinan Ozdemir for guiding us through any problem we had! As always, I had a great time building this with Neev and Shivansh, and I can't wait to continue building more things like this in the future. I'm heading to London for the next few weeks but I can't wait to get back and start building! ...more ...more

projects.title: Medify
projects.description: Medify is an AI-powered healthcare tool designed to assist soldiers and field medics in high-pressure environments. It leverages advanced machine learning to provide rapid injury assessment and tailored treatment guidance. The solution incorporates two key AI models:Wound Identification Model: Built using Python, PyTorch, and TensorFlow, this model analyzes images of injuries to classify wound types and assess severity. It ensures precise, real-time identification to guide immediate care decisions.Privacy Censorship Model: Designed for secure environments, this AI model automatically censors sensitive wound images, maintaining privacy during assessments and data sharing.Technical Details:Backend: Developed with Flask and FastAPI for seamless communication and data processing.User Interface: Built with Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS, offering a clean and intuitive design.Data Security: Utilizes blockchain technology (Midnight protocol) to encrypt and securely store data, including soldier IDs, medkit inventories, and injury details.Key Features:Efficiency: Provides rapid, AI-driven injury analysis to save critical time in emergencies.Accuracy: Tailored recommendations for treatment based on available medkit supplies.Accessibility: Text-to-speech functionality offers hands-free treatment guidance.Emergency Alerts: High-confidence injuries trigger prompts to contact emergency services.Achievements:Medify was developed to address gaps in battlefield care and empower soldiers to respond effectively in the absence of medics. It combines cutting-edge AI with a user-friendly interface, bridging the gap between field conditions and professional medical care.Impact:Medify enhances emergency response efficiency, reduces mortality rates, and ensures secure handling of sensitive data, making it an indispensable tool for military and emergency medical applications.

projects.title: FraxAI
projects.description: Fraxai is an AI-powered healthcare tool designed to assist radiologists and nurses in the emergency room. It uses advanced machine learning to streamline fracture diagnosis and treatment. The solution incorporates two key AI models:Fracture Detection Model: Built with Python, PyTorch, and Detectron2, this model analyzes X-ray images to identify fracture types and their precise locations. It highlights the fracture areas directly on the X-ray image, providing a clear visual reference.Treatment Guidance Model: Using MLflow, this model processes the detection data to generate tailored treatment instructions for nurses. It ensures that even nurses with limited training can administer accurate and effective care.Technical Details:The backend leverages a Flask REST API for communication.The user interface is built with modern web technologies, including Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS, offering an intuitive and responsive design.Key Features:Efficiency: Fraxai minimizes the time required for fracture diagnosis and treatment planning.Accuracy: Provides reliable fracture identification and treatment guidance, improving outcomes.Accessibility: Bridges the skill gap for nurses, enabling better care delivery in high-pressure environments.Achievements: Fraxai was developed during a hackathon and won "Best Freshman Hack" out of 120 participating teams, including upperclassmen. It stands out for its innovative combination of AI, practical medical applications, and a seamless user experience.Impact: By saving radiologists' time and empowering nurses, Fraxai enhances the efficiency and quality of emergency medical care.

However, discovering this content consistently is difficult. Manual feed browsing is inefficient, search results are noisy, and valuable posts are often buried beneath unrelated content. This paper presents a modular automation workflow built in n8n that supports the discovery of LinkedIn creators who publicly share workflow-based solutions. The system combines AI-assisted query generation, public Google search, structured result extraction, lightweight email pattern inference, and persistent logging. The project was developed over a period of more than three months with iterative feedback and collaboration involving both undergraduate and graduate students. Rather than acting as a ranking or recommendation system, the workflow functions as a repeatable discovery tool that reduces the time required to find creators whose workflows address common, time-consuming tasks. The results demonstrate that discovery itself can be treated as an automation problem and addressed using transparent, public, and modular systems.

publications.title: The Great Silence: An Experimental Exploration of the Fermi Paradox and Its Implications for Astrobiology
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: The Fermi Paradox, encapsulated by the question "Where are they?", highlights the profound contradiction between the high probability of extraterrestrial intelligence existing in our vast universe and the complete absence of observational evidence for such civilizations. This paper delves into the historical context of the paradox, explores its quantitative underpinnings through the Drake Equation, and rigorously examines a spectrum of hypotheses proposed to resolve this perplexing silence. We categorize these solutions into those suggesting the rarity of intelligent life, those positing the undetectability or disinterest of advanced civilizations, and those related to our own temporal position in cosmic history. Furthermore, this paper discusses the experimental dimensions of the Fermi Paradox, outlining how ongoing and future scientific endeavors, including SETI, exoplanet research, and astrobiological studies, are actively engaged in testing these hypotheses. By synthesizing current knowledge and charting pathways for future inquiry, we aim to underscore the Fermi Paradox not merely as a philosophical quandary, but as a robust driver of empirical investigation into the fundamental questions of life's prevalence and destiny in the cosmos.

publications.title: Origami-Based Kinetic and Radiative Shielding for Space Habitats: A Computational and Theoretical Investigation into Deployable Yoshimura Structures
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: The long-term human habitation of space is critically dependent on the development of lightweight, multifunctional, and deployable structures. Two of the most significant threats to crew and habitat integrity are hypervelocity impacts from micrometeoroids and orbital debris (MMOD) and the constant bombardment of galactic cosmic rays (GCR) and solar particle events (SPE). This paper presents an experimental investigation, conducted through computational simulation, into the feasibility of using an origami-based structure, specifically the Yoshimura crease pattern, as a dual-purpose shield. A Yoshimura cylinder was designed and subjected to Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to simulate its response to kinetic impacts. A separate theoretical model was developed to assess its capacity as a deployable container for radiation-shielding material. The results from the FEA simulations indicate that the Yoshimura pattern’s unique buckling mechanism effectively absorbs and distributes impact energy, reducing the risk of penetration. Furthermore, the volumetric expansion during deployment allows the structure to contain a significant mass of radiation-shielding material, increasing its areal density and protective capabilities. This research suggests that origami engineering, exemplified by the Yoshimura pattern, offers a viable and innovative solution for creating next-generation, adaptable shielding systems for future space habitats.

publications.title: Cryptocurrency and Financial Inclusion
publications.subtitle: Zenodo
publications.description: This paper examines how the adoption of Bitcoin has affected financial inclusion, banking access, and economic activity in El Salvador, with a particular focus on small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in underbanked regions. After El Salvador became the first country to recognize Bitcoin as legal tender in 2021, it created a unique opportunity to study how cryptocurrency functions outside of theory and within a real national economy. Using a mixed-methods approach, this research combines a review of academic literature, policy analysis, and media reporting with quantitative analysis of cryptocurrency market data and financial infrastructure indicators.The quantitative component includes correlation, regression, and predictive analysis of cryptocurrency price and transaction volume data, as well as an examination of Bitcoin ATM availability relative to population across major cities. These results are supported by qualitative findings that explore public adoption, SME experiences, and broader economic concerns such as volatility, infrastructure limitations, and financial stability. The findings suggest that while Bitcoin has expanded access to digital financial tools and introduced potential efficiencies in transactions, its impact on financial inclusion has been uneven, particularly in rural and underbanked areas. For SMEs, Bitcoin presents both opportunities and challenges, offering faster payments while also creating risks related to volatility, technical barriers, and implementation costs. Overall, this study highlights the mixed outcomes of cryptocurrency adoption in El Salvador and contributes to ongoing discussions about whether digital currencies can meaningfully support financial inclusion and economic development in developing economies.

my picture just went to space. literally. it was not edited onto a stock image. my photo was transmitted to SAT GUS, displayed on a Google Pixel 8 Pro aboard the satellite, and photographed with the actual Earth in the background. an idea that sounds impossible becomes real when enough talented people work together to build it. Mark Rober imagined the experience. CrunchLabs spent years turning it into reality. Tyvak, a Terran Orbital Company designed and built the SAT GUS satellite. Redwire Space, Inc. (Formerly Made In Space, Inc.) provided the specialized Argus camera used to capture the photo. SCHOTT provided the radiation-resistant glass protecting the camera system. SEOPS supported the satellite’s integration into the mission. Google Pixel provided the Pixel 8 Pro used to display each submitted picture. T-Mobile helped support and bring the project to millions of people. and on January 14, 2025, a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carried SAT GUS into orbit aboard the Transporter-12 mission. now a full year later, I have an actual picture from space. moments like this remind me that engineering is not only about machines, calculations, or technology. it is about turning curiosity into something real. something that can inspire people. something that can make space feel a little closer to all of us. Huge credit to Mark Rober , CrunchLabs , SpaceX , Tyvak, a Terran Orbital Company International, Redwire Space, Inc. (Formerly Made In Space, Inc.) , SCHOTT , SEOPS , Google Pixel, T-Mobile , and every engineer and team member who contributed to SAT GUS. this might be the coolest picture I will ever receive. 🌎🛰️

publications.title: Cultivating Multimodal Intelligence: Interpretive Reasoning and Agentic RAG Approaches to Dermatological Diagnosis
publications.subtitle: 2025 ImageCLEF MEDIQA-MAGIC Challenge (CLEF 2025)
publications.description: The 2025 ImageCLEF MEDIQA-MAGIC challenge focused on multimodal dermatology question answeringand segmentation, using real-world patient queries and images. This work addresses the Closed Visual Question Answering (CVQA) task, where the goal is to select the correct answer to multiple-choice clinical questions based on both user-submitted images and accompanying symptom descriptions.This task presents several challenges: consumer health questions are often noisy, imprecise, and lack clinical context. Unlike real-world settings where physicians can ask follow-up questions, the system must make medical decisions with high accuracy based on a single static patient interaction. This raises the difficulty of building models that generalize well and increases the risk of clinically significant misclassifications. To address these limitations, not only predictive accuracy, but also reasoning ability and explainability were prioritized. The proposed approach combines three core components: (1) fine-tuning open-source multimodal models from the Qwen, Gemma, and Llama families on the competition dataset, (2) introducing a structured reasoning layer that reconciles and adjudicates between candidate model outputs, and (3) incorporating agentic retrieval-augmented generation (agentic RAG), which adds relevant information from the American Academy of Dermatology’s symptom and condition database to fill in gaps in patient context. The team achieved second place with a submission that scored sixth, demonstrating competitive performance across both accuracy and F1 score. Beyond competitive benchmarks, this research addresses a practical challenge in telemedicine: diagnostic decisions must often be made asynchronously, with limited input and with high accuracy and interpretability. By emulating the systematic reasoning patterns employed by dermatologists when evaluating skin conditions, this architecture provided a pathway toward more reliable automated diagnostic support systems

publications.title: STORY2GAME: Generating (Almost) Everything in an Interactive Fiction Game
publications.subtitle: Preprint
publications.description: We introduce STORY2GAME, a novel approach to using Large Language Models to generate text-based interactive fiction games that starts by generating a story, populates the world, and builds the code for actions in a game engine that enables the story to play out interactively. Whereas a given set of hard-coded actions can artificially constrain story generation, the ability to generate actions means the story generation process can be more open-ended but still allow for experiences that are grounded in a game state. The key to successful action generation is to use LLM-generated preconditions and effects of actions in the stories as guides for what aspects of the game state must be tracked and changed by the game engine when a player performs an action. We also introduce a technique for dynamically generating new actions to accommodate the player's desire to perform actions that they think of that are not part of the story. Dynamic action generation may require on-the-fly updates to the game engine's state representation and revision of previously generated actions. We evaluate the success rate of action code generation with respect to whether a player can interactively play through the entire generated story.

publications.title: STARLING: Self-supervised Training of Text-based Reinforcement Learning Agent with Large Language Models
publications.subtitle: ACL Findings 2024
publications.description: Interactive fiction games have emerged as an important application to improve the generalization capabilities of language-based reinforcement learning (RL) agents. Existing environments for interactive fiction games are domain-specific or time-consuming to generate and do not train the RL agents to master a specific set of skills. In this work, we introduce an interactive environment for self-supervised RL, STARLING, for text-based games that bootstraps the text-based RL agents with automatically generated games (based on the seed set of game ideas) to boost the performance and generalization capabilities to reach a goal of the target environment. These games let the agent hone their skills on a predefined set of tasks. We create and test an environment with 100 games, generated using this automated framework that uses large language models (GPT-3) and an interactive fiction game engine (based on Inform7) to provide the user with the ability to generate more games under minimal human supervision. Experimental results based on both the human participants and baseline text-based RL agents reveal that current state-of-the-art text-based RL agents cannot use previously learned skills in new situations at the level humans can. These results enforce STARLING's potential to serve as a sandbox environment for further research in self-supervised text-based RL.

publications.title: ComplexWorld: A Large Language Model-based Interactive Fiction Learning Environment for Text-based Reinforcement Learning Agents
publications.subtitle: KBCG @ IJCAI 2023
publications.description: Interactive fiction games have emerged as an important vehicle to improve the generalization and compositional reasoning capabilities of language-based reinforcement learning (RL) agents. Existing environments for interactive fiction games are domain-specific and do not require the RL agents to utilize compositional reasoning (sequences of inter-dependent decision-making capabilities to complete a task on hand). In this work, we introduce a benchmark interactive environment, ComplexWorld, a set of text-based games that require complex composition of previously learned skills to reach a goal. These games require the agent to understand the cause-effect relationship between the intermediary decision taken towards an overarching goal. We create and test an environment with 100 complex reasoning games, generated using an automated framework that uses large language models (GPT3) and an interactive fiction game engine (based on Inform7) to provide the user with the ability to generate more games under minimal or no human supervision. Experimental results based on both the human participants and baseline text-based RL agents reveal that current state-of-the-art text-based RL agents cannot use previously learned skills in new situations involving complex reasoning at the level humans can. These results enforce ComplexWorld’s potential to serve as a sandbox environment for further research with compositional reasoning.

activity.title: What does a heart condition really look like? Not a chart. Not a diagram. Not text. But in 3 dimensions: structurally, spatially, physically. This weekend at Hacklytics'26, we built HeartScape, an interactive 3D engine that transforms segmented MRI data into explorable models, allowing users to visualize and compare healthy and diseased anatomy in real time. (Winning 3rd in Healthcare) None of us is from a medical background. That shaped our approach: not just asking how accurate the model is, but whether it’s intuitive. The computational pipeline: MRI segmentation → volumetric feature extraction → statistical modeling → PCA morphology → Vector Search → 3D mesh rendering → interactive visualization Seeing structures spatially and being able to play around with them really changes how you understand them as compared to raw data (see the transition in the images below). Massive shoutout to Shreya Chakraborty , Vehnil Rangaraman , and Atharv Singh for making this worth it! We took “follow your heart” a little too literally. This year at Hacklytics, we built HeartScape — an interactive 3D platform that transforms raw cardiac MRI data into fully explorable heart models — and I'm incredibly excited to share that we won 3rd Place for Best Healthcare Hack! Understanding congenital and structural heart disease from 2D scans is challenging, even for trained professionals. HeartScape bridges that gap by converting medical imaging data into interactive 3D models that users can rotate, slice, compare, and explore in real time. Our goal was simple: make cardiac anatomy not just visible, but truly understandable. Some of the things we built: 🫀 A pipeline that converts CMR segmentation data into lightweight 3D meshes for real-time browser rendering 🧠 AI-powered “Lens” explanations that generate contextual insights when users select regions of the heart 📊 Structural similarity search using anatomically interpretable vectors with Actian VectorAI for soft condition attribution 🔥 Point-cloud deviation heatmaps and alignment workflows powered by Sphinx.AI 🌐 A Three.js web interface for interactive exploration, annotation, and comparison between healthy and diseased hearts This project pushed us far outside our comfort zones — from learning how to interpret medical datasets (HVSMR) to building 3D geometry pipelines and integrating multiple AI systems into a cohesive experience. Absolutely loved working with Vehnil Rangaraman , Soham Agarwal , and Atharv Singh , as well as the incredible mentors and sponsors we collaborated with. What a weekend! I'm proud to share that Shreya Chakraborty and I won 𝟮𝗻𝗱 𝗣𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗲 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗹𝗹 at Hacklytics, America's largest Data Science Hackathon!! After 36 stress-inducing hours marked by sleep deprivation (red bull gives you wings) but more importantly tons of learning, Shreya and I built thera_pixel: a gamified approach to physical therapy built with ML-based motion tracking to help patients have fun while staying on pace with their recovery. Over 50 million Americans receive physical therapy services annually, however around 70% of patients do not complete their full course of care and roughly 20% drop out within the first three visits to a physical therapist. The truth is, for the average American, PT just isn't always feasible. We wanted to tackle that lack of feasibility—whether from lifestyle conflicts, affordability, or motivation hurdles—with thera_pixel. By providing engaging, responsive screen play and real-time joint position tracking, thera_pixel helps patients escape the repetitive, mundane nature of PT exercises with gamified feedback from the comfort of their homes. Using python libraries for computer vision and data processing, and MediaPipe (a Google ML-based library) for 3d Pose Estimation, we leveraged public datasets like the IntelliRehab DS (linked below) to power real-time feedback for common exercises. By temporally normalizing, interpolating, and averaging the data, we were able to create time series ground truths for key joint angles—so patients can track their accuracy and progress over time This was our first time working with core aspects of our project, like Computer Vision, Gamification, and real time Data Analysis and we learned a lot! We’re excited for where the future lies for thera_pixel and look forward to work with healthcare providers to bring it into real-world rehabilitation settings. publications.description: Contributions: Data AuditorBenchmarks are important tools for tracking the rapid advancements in large language model (LLM) capabilities. However, benchmarks are not keeping pace in difficulty: LLMs now achieve over 90\% accuracy on popular benchmarks like MMLU, limiting informed measurement of state-of-the-art LLM capabilities. In response, we introduce Humanity's Last Exam (HLE), a multi-modal benchmark at the frontier of human knowledge, designed to be the final closed-ended academic benchmark of its kind with broad subject coverage. HLE consists of 2,500 questions across dozens of subjects, including mathematics, humanities, and the natural sciences. HLE is developed globally by subject-matter experts and consists of multiple-choice and short-answer questions suitable for automated grading. Each question has a known solution that is unambiguous and easily verifiable, but cannot be quickly answered via internet retrieval. State-of-the-art LLMs demonstrate low accuracy and calibration on HLE, highlighting a significant gap between current LLM capabilities and the expert human frontier on closed-ended academic questions. To inform research and policymaking upon a clear understanding of model capabilities, we publicly release HLE at this https URL.

My first six months at UCLA were lonely. It was my first time living away from home, and I was surrounded by amazing people but couldn't seem to actually connect with any of them. I called my mom Vera Shokina every day, and she drove down from the Bay whenever she could. What I didn't know yet was that I'd already met most of the people this post is about: the ones I'd end up pulling all-nighters with, trading secrets with, and, four years later, calling my closest friends. It was just a matter for spending some more time with them. In honors calculus, I trauma-bonded with Yutian Yang (who would become my roommate for the next three years!), Julia Gu , Kuan Qian , and Karley Tioran . My next-door neighbors Hannah Kendall and Annie Feng , plus their friend Abigail Chang , became a weekly breakfast club where we'd debrief the week. Joy Cheng was one of the first people I met as a move-in assistant, and I met Surya Subbarao at a math competition (which he ended up winning!). I thought I was meeting them in passing, but four years later they're some of my best friends. When I showed up to my first LA Hacks meeting, I was disappointed to learn it was for organizing the hackathon, not competing in it. I was too embarrassed to leave. So I sat through it, realized what an incredible group of people it was, and ended up finding my biggest group of friends: Shubham Kumar , Claire Chien , Priyanshu Sharma , Anagha Srivatsav , Allison Huang , Zoey Ho , Sean Chan, Isabella Qian , Arya Bhalla , Armaan Bassi , Julie Cover , Anooshkha Shetty , Asmi K. , Sonav Agarwal , John Connell , and Tom Binford . Shubham, Sonav, John, and Tom became my go-to hackathon teammates once I started competing myself. They’ve seen me at rock bottom when I lose all hope for our project at 4am, and then in a giggle fit 5 minutes later going delirious from the sleep deprivation. I joined club track and met two of my closest friends today, Evan Leach and Nick Pavlosky . Something about feeling like you’re about to pass out after a 400 gets you really close, I guess! I bonded with Rory Hemmings, Amanda W , and Sam Gerstmann while interning in New York, and kept in touch with them once we were back at UCLA because I have the best conversations with them. I ran into Nyla Zia during a UCLA event she was organizing, and we hit it off immediately and started getting coffee together regularly. And I met with Maxine Wu, Alina Susu , Peter Nguyen , Joyce Chen , and Eric Wang through mutual friends in passing, but ended up bonding with them more deeply. To all of you, and the many others I bumped into along the way, thank you. You made me who I am now, and created memories I’ll look back at fondly for the rest of my life. UCLA, I’ll miss you!

#CVPR2026 (IEEE Technical Community on Pattern Analysis & Machine Intelligence Art Award winner) When Andrej Karpathy reproduced Yann LeCun 's 1989 network in 2022, his conclusion was that almost nothing had changed at the macro level. We still build neural networks the same way LeCun did, layers trained end to end with backpropagation, only now they are vastly bigger. Everything since has been a refinement of that 1989 template. So we rebuilt the template itself, LeNet-1, to point at the original instance of a pattern rather than one of its descendants. We rebuilt it faithfully from LeCun et al.'s NeurIPS 1989 paper, the same network he once demoed on a Bell Labs workstation, and translated only its substrate, bits into atoms. The matrices became transparent PCBs, the activations became brightness, the architecture became spatial depth you can walk around. “artefact(s): LeNet-1 (2026)” might be the oldest question we have made visible. What does it look like when something <thinks>? The work has been accepted to the CVPR 2026 Arts track and spotlighted, one of 12 works chosen from 114. I did Y Combinator with founders of Legora , Reducto , and Greptile . Today, W24 has raised close to $2 billion. Two years ago, none of us had it figured out. Nobody in that room could tell you who was going to make it. Not the partners, not the investors circling demo day, definitely not us. But I spent that batch watching the other teams, and it taught me more than most of the advice ever did. 1. The idea you apply with is rarely the one that wins. Some companies are stuck in pivot hell, trying to figure out what to build. Half the batch looked completely different by just demo day. 2. You also can't pick the winner from a demo. I was in a group with Reducto and Raindrop . Incredible founders, but on paper, none of us looked obviously destined for anything. The teams who took off just learned faster, and the market they picked mattered less. 3. The people matter more than the company. The startup you meet in the batch might not exist in a year, but the person will. It’s why the batch still pays off two years later. - Some of the founders I met in W24 are Momentic customers now. - Some have grown into people who shape what we build next. - Some are just the people I text when a six-figure deal falls apart and I need someone who actually gets it. So if you're in the batch right now: you have no idea which of you will become the next billion-dollar company. Neither did we. But be generous with the teams around you, and stay in touch long after demo day. In a couple years, any one of them could be your best customer, your closest advisor, or the only person who understands exactly what you're going through. I’m grateful I got to learn from that batch, and that two years later I still get to call some of them my closest friends.

I recently found an old article about me from when I was still a student at Berkeley, and at the time, I wrote this: “I was always entrepreneurial, but I just didn’t realize it until I reached college.” That still feels pretty accurate. I didn’t arrive at Berkeley with a five-year plan to start companies or become a venture capitalist. I just knew I liked building things, chasing ideas that seemed interesting, helping talented people achieve their potential, and bringing people together. Then, during my first semester, I entered a Berkeley entrepreneurship competition (judged by successful entrepreneurs) with an edtech idea called LectConnect and won an award. It was one of the first times I saw entrepreneurship as something I could actually do. From there, I started spending more time trying to find other student founders. There were no clubs for startups, so I decided to build the community I wished had existed when I first arrived. Reading that article again made me think about how many students are probably in the same position today. They may already have all the instincts of a founder - curiosity, ambition, a tendency to question how things work, an urge to build something better - without having a name for any of it yet. Sometimes all it takes is the right event, class, club, competition, co-founder, or community to make that possibility visible. That’s one of the things I love most about Berkeley. There are thousands of students on campus right now who haven’t figured out what they’re capable of yet. It feels great to “go for it.” Here’s me on the New Year Stock Exchange as a student in ~2011 presenting one of the top 50 startups globally at the Kairos Summit. If you’re at Berkeley and starting to build something, especially once the idea starts becoming real, reach out. You don’t need to have everything figured out. You don’t need the perfect pitch deck or a company that already looks “venture-backable.” The House Fund exists to support Berkeley founders early, and we’re always happy to be a resource - whether that means feedback, an introduction, advice, or eventually a check.

Marketing presents the coming months to sales managers, sales respond with what they are seeing in the field, and the plans that emerge are stronger for it. Introducing Biomni-Tuso, a new recipe for auto-research in biology AI model. We asked Biomni to develop a genetic perturbation prediction model and let it run for five days. It explored 500 configurations and discovered a new method that outperformed the leading methods across multiple benchmarks. We've since applied the same recipe to protein structure representation learning, enhancer–gene linking, ligand binding, and more, consistently discovering new leading models. Biomni-Tuso doesn't just tune hyperparameters. It works like an AI bio researcher for you: reading literature, thinking about orthogonal bio data sources, and testing fundamentally different modeling ideas. We believe this is where bio AI model research is headed. Instead of spending months building models by hand, researchers can describe a problem in natural language and let Biomni explore hundreds of ideas on their own data, while handling all the ML infra. Biomni-Tuso is now available as an auto-research skill (under "tusoskill") in Biomni Lab for all enterprise users. On the public platform, it is available to all users on CPU-based tasks. When I declared symbolic systems as my major six years ago, I honestly didn't really know what it meant. I liked the idea of taking classes across CS, philosophy, psych, linguistics, HCI. A clear case of decision paralysis… Sue me! By the end of my time at Stanford, it became clear to me why I gravitated toward the major. Symsys has always been about one question: how do humans and machines learn and reason? That question has shaped almost everything I've worked on. I explored it through Margins , documenting culture through fashion. Then within climate and energy, researching the infrastructure powering the AI boom. Now it's brought me to Simile ! Simile is a frontier AI lab building foundation models of human behavior. We build AI simulations grounded in real people so organizations can explore one of the hardest questions in decision making: what happens if...? What happens if we launch this product? Enter this market? Write this policy? And just as importantly, what happens if we don't? Instead of relying on limited research or intuition, organizations can rehearse consequential decisions before making them in the real world. Today, that means helping businesses make better decisions, faster. Tomorrow, the same technology could help us better understand everything from epidemic response and disaster planning to the downstream effects of economic policy. As much as this is a technical AI challenge, it's equally a design challenge. How should people interact with simulations? How do you make this new experience intuitive and delightful? And how do you know when to trust the results? Simulation sits at the intersection of machine reasoning and the messiness of human behavior, which is exactly what made me fall in love with symsys in the first place! I'm excited to be joining the GTM team, helping scale simulation across enterprises while also working on our comms and branding. It's hard to imagine a better team to invent the wheel with. Joon Sung Park , Lainie Yallen , Michael Bernstein , and Percy Liang have helped pioneer the field of generative agents, AI simulation, and foundation models. After just a few weeks here, it's clear how creative, thoughtful, and ambitious this team is. If you're as excited about the possibilities of simulation as I am, please reach out!!

The hidden talent of a Senior Director of Product Management at Meta is... Cake. Fun fact: Sean Liu builds hardware at Meta by day, and has a passion for elaborate cakes. Has even appeared on The Great American Baking Show. Last night in Palo Alto a small group sat down for dinner with folks from JZ's Product Management course at Stanford. Big tech used to come with the promise of status, scale, and certainty. An early stage startup offers power, influence, and autonomy. People (used to) pick one or the other based on where they are in their career and what they want from the next few years, and we discussed what each one of us is currently focused on. What's now changing is the shape and size of organizations and individual teams. Sean described how Meta is reorganizing around agentic orchestration. Pods of five or six people are building, each running many agents in parallel. His CTO no longer does code review. He reviews prototypes instead. Jiaona Zhang (JZ) , CPO at Laurel (previously Dropbox, Linktree, Webflow, Airbnb), is careful about headcount, focusing on a small team where everyone ships. The friction has moved from execution to coordination. The harder problem now is how humans coordinate with their agents, how pods coordinate with each other, and how to productize what these small teams can suddenly create in weeks instead of months. Where do you sit, and what are you optimizing for? And: what's your secret talent and passion project?

Sonder is my favorite word. It's this realization that every person around you is living a life as rich and complex as your own. I've been thinking about this for a while: I haven’t found a system that actually knows who I am. I use a dozen apps that each get a sliver of me. What I buy, what I listen to, where I swipe, but nothing connects the dots and knows who I am as a whole person. So I built Sondar. You talk to it. It picks up on who you are from your own words. And it finds you products, people, and experiences, all from one place that you own and control. The name is a play on sonder and sonar: deeply seeing people and picking up on subtle signals. It's very early. The intelligence is v1 and will get sharper. But the platform is live, letting people off the waitlist as they come. Check it out and tell me what hits and what doesn't. I set up this LinkedIn account years ago, but I didn't bother posting as I always assumed my network would come through the military. I started college as an Air Force ROTC cadet, and I built my identity around that path. I thrived in the structure, the discipline, the commitment to the future I thought I was stepping into. Then I was medically disqualified in late February. I accepted the news with hopes of overturning the decision, but I couldn't get it waived. My grades and my energy dipped these past two quarters, and it was humbling to realize how much of my confidence and performance came from that external structure and discipline. However, losing my original path didn’t make me smaller: it made me more well‑rounded. That identity loss was the catalyst for me to explore activities such as martial arts or bible study, and I found myself able to commit to responsibilities such as undergraduate research or club leadership. These past 4 months have taught me that people don't thrive because they're "disciplined", they thrive because of the support of those around them. If I had to sum up this chapter in a single word, it would be community. I’m deeply grateful to the people who helped me rebuild this past quarter – my family, and the cadre and cadets at Detachment 910. I also want to recognize my roommate, Matthew Kroes , for his constant support through every high and low, and Hannah Tan for welcoming me into a wonderful Christian group. I’m equally grateful to the Husky Flying Club leadership who welcomed me into my next chapter and believed in what I could contribute: • Former President – Hugh Suratgar • Former VP – Orest Brykowytch • Current President – Jack Eckhart With their support, I’m excited to share that I’ll be stepping into the role of Vice President of the Husky Flying Club. For me, the Husky Flying Club isn't just an organization that puts aircraft, pilots, and engineers in the same room. It's a community to train undergraduates to become career ready. In many ways, it's similar to ROTC. As VP, my focus this incoming school year is to prepare HFC for that mission by applying the lessons from ROTC to our club. From strengthening communication to providing opportunities for incoming members, I look forward to working with our wonderful team to build a culture structured to cultivate students. Although there is much to be done, I'm most excited about serving the community that guided me throughout my first half of university. It’s a chance to give back, support the incoming classes of aviators and engineers, and grow into the kind of leader who lifts others the way others lifted me. Cheers to the next chapter. – Albert Hengyucius

WE GOT 1ST PLACE at the Dell × NVIDIA AI Hackathon in Seattle!! 12 hours. One NVIDIA GB10. A crazy idea. And somehow… we made it happen. Going into this hackathon, I had almost no robotics experience. I came in with an idea, spent the day learning about robotics simulation, reinforcement learning, computer vision, and robot control, and started building something that felt much bigger than a weekend project. That idea became Simbiote. A local-first robotics platform that helps robots learn inside digital twins of real-world environments before being deployed into the real world. The goal was simple: What if robots could scan a space, learn in simulation, improve through human feedback, and keep sensitive data completely local? We built a pipeline that can: Turn scanned environments into simulation-ready digital twins Train robots using NVIDIA Isaac Sim + Isaac Lab Teach robots through hand-tracked teleoperation Use local AI reasoning for natural-language robot tasks The coolest part was seeing robotics, AI agents, computer vision, simulation, and local models all come together on the NVIDIA GB10. A huge thank you to my amazing teammates: Sky B. , Andrew Zhao , and Suraj Shivakumar for building this with me. Also, huge thanks to BuilderBase, Sean Chiu , the mentors, judges, organizers, and everyone who made this event possible. I'm SUPER proud to announce that my team, Gagan Shiva Kumara , Sky B. , Andrew Zhao and I have won 1ST PLACE at the NVIDIA x Dell Technologies Hackathon this weekend! 🥇🥳 We get to take home the $6,300 Dell Pro Max we developed on, with specs of an NVIDIA GB10 Blackwell GPU and 128GB of RAM. Being the great friends we are (and wanting to avoid the insane electricity bill), we're handing it over to Advaith V. for us to Remote SSH into :P Currently, robotics teams struggle to safely train and refine robots in real facilities because real‑world testing is slow, risky, and exposes sensitive environment data to external cloud services. So, with the power of the GB10, we built Simbiote: a local-first platform for training, testing, and improving robots in digital twins of real-world environments before deploying them into the real world. Our pipeline turns scanned physical spaces into simulation-ready environments, where robots can learn through reinforcement learning, receive human demonstrations through hand-tracked teleoperation, and execute natural-language tasks. Super simple to use and super effective. Our primary stack included NVIDIA Isaac Sim + Isaac Lab and PhysX for robot simulation, physics, and training; NVIDIA Nemotron for local reasoning and task planning; MediaPipe/WiLoR for hand-tracked robot control and motion; and OpenClaw for agent orchestration, guardrails, and sandboxed execution. The result: scan → simulate → train → demonstrate → improve → deploy. Our demo if you're curious: https://lnkd.in/gSbV6iq3 Massive shoutout to BuilderBase and Sean Chiu for hosting this hackathon, and all of the participants we talked with, mentors, judges, and organizers who made this event possible! And of course, our goated tablemates and ultimate moral support, Ridwan Grimes , Fuad Abdella , and Khalid M. Couldn't have done it without you. We’re sharing what we learned building automated QC for robot-mounted and ego-camera training data. A broad VLM “pass/reject” judge was difficult to calibrate. Whole-video inputs improved failure recall but produced too many false positives; sparse sampling preserved good clips but missed rare failures. The better approach was to decompose QC into failure-specific measurements. For robot video, we built focused VLM linters using temporally labeled contact sheets, explicit tail-frame sampling, and rule-specific prompts for sensor corruption, incomplete demonstrations, unrecoverable mistakes, and action overlap. For ego video, classical features won. Starting from 6,124 candidate signals, a LightGBM model using 120 features: motion, optical flow, brightness-calibrated blur, pose, hand trajectories, duration, and embedding distances reached 0.8003 out-of-time AUC across 1,777 held-out clips. DINOv2, OpenCLIP, VLM prompting, collector-history features, and stacked meta-models did not improve the final system. We’re publishing the successful approaches, failed experiments, category-level tradeoffs, and practical lessons for teams building robotics and physical AI data pipelines. The best QC model is not always the most general model. It is the one whose inputs match the failure mode. It is interesting that the headline in GPT 5.5 launch is not just what the model can do, but how many tokens it takes to do it. For a while, model capability mostly meant: can the model handle the task at all? Progress looked like bigger models, bigger context windows, more tokens, and more compute. That made sense when the main problem was simply getting useful output in the first place. But once models become broadly useful, the evaluation changes. Cost and latency stop being secondary concerns and start becoming part of the capability signal. A model that gets to the right answer in 500 tokens is meaningfully better than one that circles for 5,000 tokens before landing in the same place. The final answer may be similar, but the path matters. At scale, that path shows up in cost, latency, reliability, throughput, and user experience. So the better question is no longer: did the model get the task right? It is becoming more and more: how cleanly did it get the task right under a fixed budget of tokens, time, and context? That is one way to read “gets what to do” points to. The model reads the task correctly, uses the right tool, uses the right context, ignores what does not matter, and avoids unnecessary rambling. Part of this is the model itself becoming sharper. But part of it is also the system around the model: better harnesses, better context management, and better taste about what to include or ignore. This is why accuracy, cost, and latency should be evaluated and measured together as a combined measure of capability. The next important metric is going to be capability per token: how much useful work a model can do for a given budget of context, cost and time. The new and upcoming wave of models, benchmarks and architectures will be judged this way. It's going to be better outcomes with fewer wasted tokens, for everyone. At Mem0 , this is how we already think about memory systems and benchmarks. Our new algorithm is a step toward making capability per token a standard way to evaluate memory in production.

Our latest In Context newsletter breaks down BEAM, the memory benchmark that tests AI agents at up to 10M tokens, based on “Beyond a Million Tokens: Benchmarking and Enhancing Long-Term Memory in LLMs” (ICLR 2026). Full breakdown ↓

We recently released a token-efficient memory algorithm for agents at Mem0 . Our latest memory system achieves 91.6 on LoCoMo, 93.4 on LongMemEval, and 64.1 / 48.6 on BEAM (1M / 10M), while averaging < 7,000 tokens per retrieval call, at 3–4x lower token cost. Typically, full-context approaches on these benchmarks typically run at 25,000+ tokens. What this means for developers: you can run agent memory that is cost-efficient at production scale without sacrificing quality. The goal was to make memory work under real-world constraints, limited context windows, latency budgets, and production scale. What changed: - Single-pass, add-only extraction (~50% faster) - Agent-generated facts treated as first-class - Entity linking across people, places, and concepts - Multi-signal retrieval (semantic + keyword + entity) - Keyword normalization for better recall Full evaluation framework is open source. Available today on our platform and open-source SDK https://mem0.ai/research

Introducing Mem0 CLI A way to give your agents memory directly from the terminal. As agents become more capable, one thing is still missing: they don’t remember. At Mem0 , we believe memory is the missing layer for stateful AI systems. That’s why we built mem0 CLI, you can: - Add, search, and retrieve memory - Store preferences across agents and users - Persist context beyond a single session - Work with structured, schema-driven (JSON) memory Just plug it in, and your agents start remembering. This is designed for both: - Developers building agent workflows - Agents that need to manage their own memory We’re excited about what this unlocks: more personalized, context-aware, and stateful AI systems. Get started: npm install -g @mem0/cli Open source ↓

Yesterday, We took over NVIDIA GTC. We showed up with 5,000 cold water bottles and people in Mem0 swag at every corner. NVIDIA GTC is the Super Bowl of AI conferences. So instead of paying $50,000 for a sponsorship seat and just another branded taxi, we showed up IRL. Real people, real conversations, real laughs, and something that people needed: Cold water in 90° weather and some Jensen Huang slander on a t-shirt. The reactions: "Mem0 is literally everywhere." I just wrapped up my summer internship at USC’s Information Sciences Institute, where I worked on SPHERE Research Infrastructure , a national testbed for reproducible cybersecurity experimentation. My role involved taking published research artifacts from venues including IEEE S&P, USENIX Security, ACSAC, NDSS, and PETS and getting them running on SPHERE so that other researchers could redeploy and verify them. It sounds straightforward. It is not. What I did not expect was that the hardest failures would be the quiet ones: scripts that report success while producing empty output files, a locale setting that silently corrupts results, or a configuration path with the wrong quotation marks that fills a disk without warning until the build fails 40 minutes later. Almost nothing announced itself as broken. Another major lesson was that testing on the machine you built on proves very little. A development node accumulates state that your installation script never had to earn. The real test is deploying on a fresh node from scratch, and that exposed gaps every single time. Reproducibility is often discussed as a research virtue. Up close, it is mostly unglamorous debugging, careful documentation, and being honest when something does not reproduce, then clearly documenting why. Thank you to Jelena Mirkovic , David Balenson , and the SPHERE Research Infrastructure team for their guidance. And thank you to my fellow interns, Allison Lu , Yizhu Wen , Prathyush Turaga, and Sonali Singh, for making a summer full of stack traces genuinely fun.

That’s a wrap on the 2026 SPHERE summer internship program! This year, 23 interns worked with SPHERE, including 18 students onsite with our teams at USC Information Sciences Institute , Northeastern University , and the University of Utah , and five virtual interns. Over the summer, they made real contributions to SPHERE, working on projects ranging from IoT and industrial control systems to experiment automation, reusable research artifacts, and the software and operations that keep the testbed running. They capped off the summer by presenting their work at our 2026 SPHERE Intern Showcase. We’re grateful to all of our interns for their hard work, creativity, and enthusiasm, and to the SPHERE team members who mentored them throughout the summer. We wish them all the best in their studies, research, and whatever comes next! Their work also helps make SPHERE a more capable and useful research infrastructure for the broader cybersecurity and privacy community. We’re excited to build on their contributions as SPHERE continues to grow with support from the National Science Foundation (NSF) Science Foundation. #SPHERE #Cybersecurity #Privacy #ResearchInfrastructure #Internships

Today we introduce Maple-Preview, an open-source 20B-A1B ternary-weight reasoning LLM, SOTA in its weight class. Maple-Preview can solve IMO-level problems and runs at over 200 tokens/sec on an M4 Mac Mini, 5–16x faster than efficient models like Gemma 4, Qwen3.5, and gpt-oss. Maple-Preview's light footprint enables on-device adaptation, made possible by the model's speed, energy, and memory efficiency. In early experiments, Maple-Preview is able to learn on the fly while running locally on a MacBook Pro. It autonomously decides which facts and user preferences to remember and then "dreams" about them later to embed that knowledge into its weights. This approach helps the model retain subtle, user-specific details that text-based memories may miss and addresses the scalability challenges of growing context. We believe that in the future, edge models will learn preferences by adapting their weights rather than through thousands of facts scattered across .md files, embedding user preferences into their own truly personal agent. At DeepGrove, we study how efficient models learn, rethinking architecture, training infrastructure, optimization, and hardware design to treat low precision as a first-class citizen. I recently took up a temporary part-time retail sales role, and it gave me an unexpected reminder that user experience (UX) is not just about websites or apps. UX exists in the physical store, the product display, the staff onboarding process, the point-of-sale (POS) workflow, the stock system, the product catalogue, and the way customers are guided from “just browsing” to finding something meaningful. What stood out to me was the contrast between the in-store customer experience and the digital version. In-store, new customers often began with curiosity. They were first drawn in by the window display, then browsed curated displays, noticed colour groupings, and slowly discovered the collections through the narrative shared by the sales team. That journey felt natural: visual attraction first, then curiosity, then story, then product consideration. Online, many e-commerce websites do the reverse. They open like catalogues: product grids, categories, collection names, filters, prices. That may be efficient for returning customers, but for someone new to the brand, it can feel transactional, especially when the brand’s real strength lies in storytelling, craftsmanship, place, and emotional discovery. It made me ask: How might we make a website feel less like “shop all products” and more like “step into the store”? A stronger digital experience could mirror the physical journey: Starting with a visual window display, the customers browse through the "rooms"; ultimately the craft and brand story are brought into the discovery flow. At the same time, the role also made me think about the internal UX. As a newcomer with no retail sales training, I noticed much of the operational knowledge lived informally in people’s heads: product characteristics, selling points, pairing logic, stock quirks, bundle deals and “how things are usually done.” When onboarding depends mostly on verbal guidance and memory, mistakes become more likely — not because people are careless or less capable, but because the system has not made the right information visible at the right moment. This was especially clear at checkout, where bundle deals had to be remembered, checked for eligibility, and keyed in manually as custom POS discounts — all while keeping the customer experience smooth. That is also UX. Good design reduces guesswork. It supports new staff by making hidden knowledge visible. It helps people serve customers consistently without relying entirely on memory, assumptions, or whoever happens to be present that day. The biggest takeaway for me: customer experience and employee experience are deeply connected. A polished customer-facing journey is hard to sustain when the behind-the-scenes systems are unclear, undocumented, or unsupported. Design is not only what the customer sees. It is the system that helps people care, choose, serve, and connect.

Why I Said "No" to a Full-Time Offer to Say "Yes" to Self-Investment. I recently received a full-time job offer. On paper, it was a step up in structure and workflow compared to my most recent experience. Yet, the final compensation package landed about 8% below my expected anchor. In the past, the conventional corporate script would dictate standard negotiation tactics, or perhaps a compromise to secure the predictability of a monthly paycheck. Instead, I chose to bow out graciously. Stepping away made me realise a profound truth: We often focus so much on the market value companies place on us, that we forget to calculate the value we place on our own time. For 20 years, my prime was dedicated entirely to raising a beautiful family and managing caregiving responsibilities. Now that my home base is settled and those heavy seasons have naturally concluded, I find myself in a rare, vibrant window of life. By declining an offer that did not fully align, I did not lose an opportunity. I chose to keep complete control of my time—and invest it directly back into myself. What I have realised is that skills do not expire just because you step away from a corporate desk. The analytical training from my university years and the strategic navigation required during my working life did not vanish; they simply transferred. Lately, I have been applying that foundational problem solving toolkit to run my own personal "growth accelerator," driven by trial, error, and curiosity: Mental Fitness: To push through the steep curves of mastering Japanese while being mindful of budget and to re-visit conversational Korean to prepare for an upcoming trip. Creative Frictions: Using systematic trial-and-error to discover the precision and patience required for artisan bread making and flower arrangement. Physical Strength: Staying disciplined with structured fitness classes and heavy compound lifting at the gym. Up next on the horizon? Setting up violin lessons to introduce a completely new layer of creative challenge. True mental stimulation and critical thinking do not happen only within a 9-to-5 frame. They happen when you give your brain the freedom to adapt, fail, learn, and create using the lifetime of skills you've already built. If you are currently navigating a career transition or stepping into a new chapter of life, remember this: You are not "underemployed" if you are actively self-invested. Don't be afraid to own your time, leverage your foundational strengths, and build a life portfolio that actually fulfills you. #CareerTransitions #SelfInvestment #ContinuousLearning #PersonalGrowth #MidLifeRenaissance #WorkLifeDesign
